Decision trees are widely used in various applications due to their effectiveness and ease of interpretation. However, optimizing decision trees remains a challenging problem, especially when trying to avoid local minima and identify the best possible structure. Traditional decision tree learning methods rely on heuristics that limit their scope to known features, excluding valuable zero-shot knowledge. In this study, we investigate the potential of decision rules learned from decision-based model training data to provide useful, instance-specific information even when the underlying model is unknown. We demonstrate that these rules can effectively guide the generation of training samples, allowing for the construction of decision tree models that outperform traditional random forest architectures when applied to new, unseen data. Our approach is evaluated through experiments on real-world datasets, showcasing the value of zero-shot knowledge transfer in decision tree learning.

Given the submodules of a lattice of modules in a group or an algebra, we can visualize their inclusion relationships as a Hasse diagram. Specifically, we are examining this lattice of modules for the symmetric group in relation to its Young subgroup, denoted as $S_n \wr S_2$. We present an efficient method to construct this lattice of submodules based on just two inputs: the submodules of $S_n$ that are invariant under $S_2$ and the lattice of submodules of a single element within the group. Consequently, we can apply this lattice construction to other symmetric groups beyond $S_n$.

Reinforcement learning systems improve significantly when they are initially pre-trained. To further accelerate learning when an agent is provided with imitation data, it's essential to equip the model with task-related prior knowledge. However, in many instances, it's不明朗 whether simple supervised learning imitation is sufficient due to the abundance of available demonstrations. In this study, we developed a Co-Imitation Training framework, in which the model is taught to learn from both accurate and opposite actions of the task at hand. Although our initial results were comparable to those of imitation learning, our Co-Imitation model achieved a 1.5 times superior performance on tasks that were not previously seen, when only minimal tuning was applied.

This paper fills in metrics related to PAC codes and establishes their relationship to Guava's code distance function. We demonstrate that the distance between zero and a specific code c is equivalent to the weight of c, and also provide a metric for determining the distance between two codes. Furthermore, we provide step-by-step calculations of the distances between the PAC codes and the code representing the English language.

We investigate the use of reinforcement learning techniques for enhancing the performance of neural machine translation models, focusing on reducing translation errors measured by BLEU metrics. To achieve this, we developed two unconventional, high-cost action spaces for refining model predictions: an exploration space, which involves selectively amplifying and shifting token probabilities to introduce variability, and a extraction space, which targets and removing specific parts of the translation to facilitate easier correction. Our findings demonstrate that this framework leads to models that consistently outperform the standard training method, yielding improvements of roughly 0.5 BLEU in multiple scenarios.

The study of open quantum systems under Markovian dynamics is intriguing because, in most cases, it leads to a stable, non-equilibrium state known as a steady state, which is reached regardless of the initial state. This research paper introduces an in-depth, combined experimental and theoretical investigation of the dynamics of an open two-level system, resulting from the interplay between a driven coherent element and several environments. By utilizing advanced techniques for creating and measuring this system's complex dynamic behavior, we successfully replicated and went beyond our previous observations to accurately describe the path to reaching a stable, non-equilibrium state. Our successful model uses competing decay processes consisting of population suppression and excitation.

We explore various bi-linear maps in the euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ for $n \ge 2$, including De, Shape, and Laplacian operators, introducing the concept of recurrent structures via these maps. Our analysis indicates that any submanifold possessing a de-recurrent structure in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ must be a de-flat hypersurface. Similarly, bi-recurrent and tri-recurrent configurations are proven to be inherently de-recurrent and de-flat. Furthermore, specific conditions under which de-recurrent and de-flat structures occur are proven to include hypersurfaces composed of circular paths within the euclidean space. However, it is established that de-recurrent and de-flat structures do not exist for compact submanifolds in the euclidean space, whereas all hypersurfaces with constant de curvature $E$, where $E$ represents any combination of operators from {De, Shape, Laplacian}, must be manifolds with constant curvature in the euclidean space.

A set of strings is called $p/q$-identifiable from observations $p/q$-distinct from each other if a probabilistic algorithm can accurately determine whether it belongs to the set based on a single, unique sample from the set, but is unable to do so without a specific ratio of additional samples to classification errors that decreases as the complexity of the task increases given only non-unique distributions. This concept is related to standard identifiability and mutual identifiability, but differs in its treatment of the relationship between the complexity of the task and the complexity of the classifier.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that facilitates coherent application-level transactions across its sharded clusters. Our investigation reveals that MongoDB's application-level transaction coherence model deviates from the standard definition of transactional coherence established by Bernstein et al. (1987). Through our work, we provide formal definitions for both MongoDB's consistency model and transactional coherence, along with verification techniques using Coq, showing that its consistency model guarantees transactional coherence, even in environments with sharding.

Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three, finding a coefficient that is positively coefficient-wise divisible by the elementary symmetric function with non-negative integer coefficients forming an inverse Kostka matrix. This result extends a previous result by Hance, Le, and Sagan who proved the $e$-positivity of the chromatic symmetric functions for Dyck paths with a bounce number of two using the same inverse Kostka matrix.

Research on concealed geometric structures within complex networks has recently gained significant attention. To uncover these hidden patterns and their effect on network dynamics, we examined a model featuring a collection of nanoscale triangular assemblies with either bond randomness or bimodal distributions. In this model, triangle-to-triangle connectivity can create a concealed triangular lattice within the network of nanassemblies. By simulating the spin reversal dynamics of a model complex nanassemblies with both open and closed configurations, and investigating the impact of geometric structure on dynamics, our findings reveal that the lattice-based interactions result in distinct characteristics of magnetization reversal and the emergence of a novel phenomenon known as the three-step hysteresis effect.

The theories and practical needs for inner solar system energy harvesting both depend on a deeper understanding of the solar wind's energy flux in this region, alongside the structures and movement of magnetic fields. The recent launch of the Parker Solar Probe, a mission designed to break records, enables groundbreaking research into solar wind dynamics through inner 0.25 AU of the heliosphere. The spacecraft is set to collect detailed data on the energy flux and magnetic field configurations in the first six years, and plan updates aim to enhance trajectory efficiency for optimal energy gathering potential along its path. The initial observations from the PSR instrument on the PSP spacecraft, which will break records in close approaches to the Sun, also promise to provide unique insights into the structure and variability of solar wind around the Sun. The first six months of observations, covering the outer heliosphere, span over ten orders of magnitude in energy flux density, reflecting the complex structure of the solar wind and requiring further analysis to fully interpret. The study of solar wind energy flux density fluctuations is essential for understanding the factors contributing to their formation and for accurately predicting space weather events.

The emotion identification field has undergone significant advancement in recent years, although considerable challenge persists in accurately detecting emotions within speech. The problem is further compounded by the prevalence of datasets that are inadequate in terms of both the emotional content they cover and their representation of a diverse range of speakers and genders. In an attempt to accurately assess current methodologies and models, we introduce a new dataset comprised of ten speakers and five distinct emotions, although it is acknowledged in relation to existing data that the number of speakers and genders present is still limited. Building on this constraint, we propose a solution involving a deep reinforcement learning-based domain adaptation strategy to effectively transfer training from fabricated datasets to those with fewer speakers and genders. Ultimately, the combination of a new dataset and the proposed solution aims to make progress towards a more equitable and inclusive emotion identification field.

Researchers studying an eternally expanding universe began modeling a spherical void and found that, under specific initial conditions within a part of parameter space, the model eventually collapsed and created a "white hole" within the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker framework.

This study aims to determine the differential decay rate structure of $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ by collecting $3.0\times 10^5$ reconstructed signal candidates from L3 and L0 channels with an average muon detection efficiency of 16%. 
Furthermore, three key parameters defining the differential decay rate structure have been estimated for the first time from LHCb data. 
Alternatively, using previously established results from other experiments, the differential decay rate form can be modeled with an impact parameter distribution from $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ decays. 
The obtained differential decay rate structure is consistent with theoretical predictions from lattice QCD.

A recent paper provides an analysis of research conducted by Aomaki and Ito regarding Schrödinger operators with specific characteristics. We establish a link between these operators and a broader class of polynomial solutions in quantum mechanics, including both standard and generalized Hermite polynomials. We also explore the connection between generalized Hermite polynomials and Laguerre-Hopf polynomials, as well as their hypergeometric representations. Additionally, we derive a corresponding network of polynomial relationships, mirroring those of the Aomaki-Ito operators. We further investigate the monodromy properties of these polynomials in the complex plane and their associated Riemann surfaces. Ultimately, we introduce a comprehensive framework for understanding Schrödinger operators with the specified characteristics based on the aforementioned polynomial relationships.

A noisy sound is made when adhesive tape peels back at a consistent rate, and the sound's frequency characteristics have been studied using the power spectral density (PSD). The PSD shows two distinct parts: a noisy section related to random events and a structured section shaped like a power law. The structured section's slope has been observed to change depending on factors like peeling speed, measurement methods, and experimental conditions, but these variations have been directly linked to the physical properties of the process in recent studies. However, in our study, we found the PSD slope to suddenly and unpredictably change during the tape peeling process at a constant speed, which was found to be related to local surface reflections at certain frequencies. As this finding is unrelated to the sound generation process, we developed a correction method that accounts for these reflections to reveal new information about the tape peeling process, including its stick-slip behavior.

Recently, a novel theory was proposed that modified Maxwell's electrodynamics by adding a spatial preference term, effectively an 'ether' term that is visualized as cubes floating in space. This concept was then re-examined by integrating statistical mechanics and quantum field theory, but this time for the ether term that follows the Bose-Einstein distribution law rather than behaving as a fixed, classical term. This thermal variation of the ether term was found to significantly change the behavior of the ether-term Hall effect, this effect is visualized in Figure one where the main features of the non-abelian thermal ether-like term are presented. It is found that the non-abelian thermal term causes the critical temperature and the upper critical temperature to shift, this shift is relevant in describing superconductivity. Consequently, this non-abelian thermal term is proposed to serve as an effective approach to the high-temperature superconductivity phenomenon.

This research develops a method for determining the optimal option margin by considering the cost of option delta hedging and unhedged delta risk. The study uses a stochastic control approach to find the ideal margin and confirms the validity of the derived equation through the Lenskens et al. (2019) approach. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this equation can be applied to practical scenarios, such as pricing European options on non-dividend paying assets and money option calls, and provide corresponding code for implementation in R and Python.

Our dynamic economic growth framework highlights the significance of intergenerational mobility in shaping long-term societal development. Given its mobility's variable nature across different groups, we propose exploring the benefits of distributing intergenerational mobility opportunities evenly throughout society in order to maximize long-term development. Our research reveals that implementing such an equitable mobility policy results in a significant increase in the rate of technological advancement and per capita development, surpassing current methods that prioritize high-income generation. Furthermore, our proposed equitable mobility strategy also reduces population disparities, thereby creating a more balanced society.

A scan of the brightness distribution of a beam is a fundamental way to characterize its phase space distribution. This basic approach has been primarily used to make small corrections to beam properties, but now it is applied to thoroughly study a significant resonance in the BEPCII horizontal plane, identifying a significant discrepancy between measured and predicted resonance shapes.

This paper explores an optimized algorithm for multi-agent systems through the use of a distributed optimization method that avoids the need for agents to exchange heavily sized data. The proposed method achieves the same results as the optimized algorithm through the use of rounded numerical values in a networked environment. The method is applicable in various fields including signal processing, telecommunications and machine learning.

A new Python library called s4cmb has been developed to integrate the PySM code for cosmological simulations, specifically to account for instrumental effects on Cosmic Microwave Background data. This integration enables users to easily visualize the impact of instrumental effects on various experiments, including Planck, WMAP, SIMBOLEO, and SIMONE. Unlike previous PySM simulations, which overly broadened temperature power spectra in k-space, this revised approach correctly represents the distortion of temperature and polarization maps, ultimately affecting observed temperature and polarization auto- and cross-spectra.

In the task of arranging unordered words into correct sequences, prior approaches rely on discriminative models that use already-processed language representations, leveraging neural networks and attention mechanisms. Leveraging pre-trained language models like BART, our research explores their potential in solving sequence reconstruction problems. We found that models like BART can be fine-tuned to achieve state-of-the-art results on widely-used language understanding datasets such as SQuAD and SQuAD 2.0 S. Ramachandran, Y. Kim, and J. Esteva's work, particularly in low-data scenarios. Furthermore, BART's performance excels on complex multi-token answers and is capable of reconstructing sentences from natural language queries. Our analysis also reveals that sequence reconstruction is integral to the internal workings of transformer-based models like BART. In contrast to models based on maximum likelihood reasoning, we found that BART's attention patterns are more aligned with its reconstruction capabilities than its fundamental reasoning. This work highlights the potential for using large, pre-trained language models like BART effectively in a variety of natural language understanding applications.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media on social platforms has given rise to the prevalence of deepfakes, which have also sparked extensive research. The ever-changing and heterogeneous regulations along with research communities across different jurisdictions have yielded a multitude of deepfake detection methods. In this context, our survey of these methods reveals that numerous countries are producing numerous models for deepfake detection, each with distinct architectures. Consequently, this diversity presents a challenge in terms of generalization ability. To address this challenge, our work proposes the MD-CSDNetwork, an innovative detection framework for multiple deepfake models. This framework comprises two key components, namely knowledge distillation modules and cross-stitch networks. The knowledge distillation modules enable our network to capture general detection knowledge from multiple models, while the cross-stitch networks facilitate interaction between the knowledge modules and the models' features. As demonstrated in our experiments, our network achieves state-of-the-art performance on cross-dataset evaluation using the FaceForeniscs' dataset as the source of real video footage, while also showing efficiency gains in terms of training time and parameter count.

In 1930, mathematician Menger developed the concept of metric spaces characterized by specific metrics that locally resemble Euclidean geometry. These are known as metric spaces with local metric properties. While studying these structures, Menger identified two essential conditions he believed were both necessary and sufficient for a metric space to be considered a Euclidean space with a specific dimensionality. However, it was later discovered that his initial formulation of these conditions was inaccurate, and this correction was made by his former students. Specifically, three researchers proved that rather than being sufficient to define Euclidean geometry, these conditions are actually indicative of a different mathematical structure known as a CAT(0) space or a space containing no triangles with curvature greater than zero. Ultimately, this is in contrast to CAT(k) spaces or space containing no spheres with curvature greater than zero, which would indicate a space with specific curvature properties.

Consider a number field K of degree n over the rational numbers Q, equipped with a basis $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n$, and the associated successive minima $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$ relative to the field norm. In this report, we establish upper and lower constraints on the ratios of consecutive minima, specifically $\lambda_{i+1}/\lambda_i$ for $i=1, \dots, n-1$. We compare these findings with a previous upper bound proposed by Lehmer in 1954. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between these minima and the geometric properties of a curve defined over the real numbers, demonstrating upper bounds on the coefficients of its Hermite-Siegel invariants, with specific examples illustrating lower bounds on some of our estimates.

Using a cluster algebra framework, we establish the Fock-Vershik representation of the quantum group $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_2)$ at the level of the space of vertex operator representations. This finding builds upon earlier work by Geer-Ruiz and Le-Moizey for non-primeness level $p \geq 5$. Furthermore, we observe the inapplicability of our result at the level $p=3$. Moreover, we apply and extend a result from Berenstein-Sassoon regarding the cluster nature of the affine Lie algebra at the level three, incorporating input from Le's work on the three-fold tensor property at level three.

For the first time, our research delves into the complexities of the Forsage yield pyramid scheme, which caused over $280 million in losses for its victims according to DdLab. Forsage was particularly deceptive as it masked its pyramid scheme nature for over a month, during which $20 million worth of funds were transferred, despite its code being freely available online. Our study examines the Forsage protocol's architecture, including the intricate state machine and financial mechanisms it employs to conceal its fraudulent practices. Furthermore, we analyze the Forsage marketing strategy, which targeted social media users with a referral-based Ticker game that rewarded players for referring new participants. Unfortunately, this design led to the scheme's rapid discovery, prompting us to propose enhanced privacy-preserving designs for pyramid schemes. Our analysis is based on the Forsage code, transaction records, public announcements, and interviews with its developers.

We identified potential new luminosity functions for the galaxy, including 19 cluster candidates from 44 GBP sample clusters presented in VVV. Each potential cluster's properties were extracted from the VVV data, converting the outputs to standard formats. We compared their metallicities and the ratio of iron to titanium elements across the four known Milky Way populations. Four of the clusters exhibit low metallicities similar to open cluster fields, six have low to intermediate metallicities, four have intermediate metallicities, and eight have a high ratio of iron to titanium. Additionally, we plotted their positions relative to the globular cluster sequence and found they mostly fall into regions associated with known globular clusters, except for one outlier VVVIR205 with very low metallicities and a high iron to titanium ratio. VVVIR205 is unlike any other known galaxy population.

This research reveals a significant transformation in holographic error correction codes when uniform superpositions are applied to classical binary graphs, revealing hyper-invariant max-flip and hyper-rotationally invariant phase-flip operations. These discoveries facilitate the development of efficient algorithms for calculating entanglement entropy and quantum dimensions. By utilizing these findings, we were able to create an enhanced holographic code, referred to as hyper-MERA, with a novel structure that provides a continuous, scale-free, and isotropic representation of spin systems through classical reversible circuits. This code's unique characteristics enable the preservation of local Ising model dynamics, thus yielding the Mutually Information Scale (MIS) for this system. Furthermore, our study presents an in-depth mathematical and numerical investigation of the associated MIS tensor and its underlying dynamics, comparing our discoveries to previous research.

Deep-learning methods such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent Neural
Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications. In our study, we
investigate how deep-learning approaches can be used to both uncover patterns and forecast
future process outcomes. We focus specifically on discovering exceptions and forecasting
deviations from expected processes. Our experiments reveal that deep-learning techniques
can effectively identify process exceptions by leveraging probabilistic models to detect
anomalies. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these exceptions can be used to predict
process failures ahead of time. Our findings provide a practical pathway for using
data-mining techniques to flag and predict process anomalies.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The study also includes computations of these parameters for specific examples, including Toeplitz transformations of multivariate polynomials and multivariate Gaussian functions, where they do or do not meet certain conditions.

An investigation into the chromosphere during solar flares is conducted, focusing on a massive flare, designating it as X4.1, associated with the star Ad Leo on the main sequence with an mass of 22 percent of the Sun's mass, in an active binary system known as AM Persei B, in 1985. A theoretical model of the chromosphere is developed, utilizing a non-LTE radiative transfer approach, in an attempt to replicate the near-ultraviolet spectral data obtained from the IUE space observatory in the 380 to 1850 Angstrom range during the flare's maximum intensity. The model incorporates the effects of hydrogen and helium resonance and intercombination lines as well as charge exchange processes designed to account for observed features such as the broadening and blue-shift of HLyman-alpha and HeII Lyman-alpha lines, in addition to the saturation of the HBr gamma line.

Neural rendering technology has made significant progress with 3D point cloud models, but current approaches primarily handle point cloud formats such as LiDAR and camera fusion. These models struggle to generalize when applied to synthetic data with geometric shapes. Our research focuses on creating a highly compact neural renderer that can accurately render diverse 3D point cloud scenes, including real-world objects and complex, multi-object environments. To achieve this, we develop a novel training framework, called TPC (Transformation-Unique Point Cloud Smoothing), utilizing a set of point cloud transformations to prevent potential ambiguities in the model's learning process. Experimental results show that TPC yields notable improvements, accurately replicating both singular and aggregated scenes over state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the TPC framework demonstrates versatility, successfully generalizing to other point cloud models and facilitating efficient, large-scale training. Our publication is available at https://tpc-renderer.github.io/.

This study employs the Jost function approach within the Random Phase Approximation (RPA) framework to investigate the electric quadrupole resonance (GDR) for oxygen-16. A key finding of our research is the confirmation of the intricate nature of the GDR's energy, which behaves similarly to a cut in the complex energy plane, indicating a sign of resonance in the real energy region. Furthermore, we have successfully replicated the Gaussian shape of the GDR's strength distribution, which has a width of 4.1 MeV and a central energy of 25.0 MeV. Additionally, we have determined the RPA response function in the energy domain.

In high-dimensional spatial datasets, particularly those derived from dynamical systems, identifying clusters with interpretive value poses a significant challenge. Traditional unsupervised clustering techniques often fail in such contexts due to the intricate and evolving nature of the underlying dynamics. We introduce an innovative approach, Impact Based Clustering (IBC), tailored specifically for dynamical systems represented in phase space. Rather than relying on geometric cluster definitions, our method partitions space based on the anticipated behavior of dynamics in a forthcoming time period. IBC achieves this by integrating a machine learning model with a parameter of interest and utilizing simulation filters to efficiently process large datasets. In addition to being adaptable to various systems and preserving the statistical properties of the underlying distribution, IBC demonstrates higher efficiency in comparison to conventional methods, geometrically breaking the timescale barrier in cosmological simulations by a factor of 100. IBC successfully processes large datasets with a number of parameters a which it can simultaneously cluster, setting a potential benchmark for future high-dimensional clustering applications.

Deep neural networks for language generation rely on dense vector representations, which contain excessive information and many redundant elements. Although recent sparse modeling techniques have achieved positive results in various tasks such as classification, they fall short in generating high-quality text. In our work, we draw inspiration from the Generative Adversarial Network framework to develop the SparseGAN model, which generates a single word at a time while maintaining a sparse state represented by multiple latent vectors. We propose three key advantages of utilizing sparse modeling in the generative process: it makes capturing complex word sequences easier, enhances the interpretability of the model, and facilitates efficient inference. Experimental evaluations on several datasets including GMAN, IM, and WebText demonstrate that our model outperforms existing methods in terms of overall generation quality, further validated by human assessments. Moreover, human feedback reveals that sparse modeling improves the model's ability to grasp complex sentence structures, interpretability of generated texts, and inference efficiency while yielding comparable results in terms of grammatical correctness and fluency. Our code is publicly accessible at the following link: this GitHub repository.

The theory of interstellar Panspermia posits that microbial life could be transferred between galaxies, with the key consideration being whether such organisms survive the harsh journey. Using first principles, we position ourselves in an interstellar void, surrounded by a stream of high-speed particles and sparse gases, to assess the feasibility of detecting these "passengers" from outside. We consider various aspects of this environment that could be observed, including the re-emission of light, temporary changes in how starlight is absorbed, and distortions in radio wave signals. However, despite various suggestions, we find that these effects are too minute to be measurable with current technology, thus highlighting the limitations of discovering life carried on rocky bodies through the vastness of space.

Animal population studies often ignore an animal's specific resource requirements, 
which can significantly impact their movement, access to essential resources like 
partners or food, and overall source of information for animal population studies. 
To address this issue, our paper proposes a statistical model for capture data that 
incorporates an animal's access to specific sources, such as their spatial activity 
range or required resources, at the time of capture, which will significantly help 
researchers to estimate the probability of animal capture and source abundance more 
effectively. Our study also presents an example of applying this model to data 
collected from beavers and proposes various directions for future research.

The dynamics of oscillators within multi-layer networks can be influenced by their tendency to synchronize across various connections. We've now expanded the concept of solution transmission to encompass these multilayer networks, building on a previously defined notion from simpler networks. Our research focuses on the interaction between the concept of transmitted solutions and the stability of synchronization in multilayer networks, utilizing a specific model with two coupled layers to conduct detailed analysis. Our findings reveal that networks with a higher degree of multilayer connectivity tend to produce more robust synchronization, and that transmitted solutions play a crucial functional role in the overall dynamics. Moreover, we've explored the impact of connecting phase nodes and found that their position and the direction of connections can significantly affect the stability of synchronization in such networks.

A causal constitutive material model is represented mathematically by the Cauchy stress operator, which is analyzed for its fundamental properties. This operator is characterized by four key properties: objectivity, material frame-indifference, coercivity, and the principle of supply. The constitutive responses of both hyperelastic and non-hyperelastic materials are parameterized using the Generalized Storage Function. However, this approach fails to encompass all materials due to its foundation in a specific energy density. An alternative approach based on the Cauchy stress operator is proposed, which can describe all constitutive responses. This approach is based on two fundamental building blocks: a storage operator and a descent operator. The application of these building blocks is demonstrated in the context of linear and nonlinear hyperelasticity. Additionally, the relevant literature is reviewed.

The integration of formal verification and testing offers a more cost-effective and early bug detection method compared to purely formal or traditional testing approaches. However, a unifying theoretical framework that combines testing and analysis is still missing. Our research Integro presents a novel geometric approach for test generation that identifies programs as functions within a set of mathematical objects, specifically functions mapping inputs to outputs, and generates tests based on the properties of these objects. Integro's framework enables the automatic generation of tests with specific characteristics, and we've initially implemented this framework, showcasing its capability to generate tests for various program types, including atomic operations, composite programs, and even parsed code, as demonstrated in this technical report.

This paper is a discussion of several interesting findings related to vector fields that adhere to the equation $|\sum_{j=1}^k \langle v_j,x\rangle|^2\le 1-x^2,$ where $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ denotes a specific type of inner product defined on the space. These vector fields are common in different mathematical and physical contexts, including Euclidean geometry, complex numbers, quaternions, and octonions. We provide circular arrangements for vectors in certain representations of these algebraic structures. Notably, this research extends previous findings by Jamison in 1966, proving that for specific complex matrix representations, the maximum number of vectors that can be formed in $\mathbb{C}^m$ is equal to the dimension of the algebraic structure, regardless of the value of $m$. The study also includes an analysis of possible configurations of vectors within the algebraic structure of exceptional Lie algebra $E_8$.

Creating large-scale maps of underground infrastructure networks is essential for ensuring safety during urban development and drone operations. These maps help avoid collisions and accidents by identifying areas filled with underground tunnels. One critical factor in developing an accurate, comprehensive 3D representation of these networks is determining their spatial extent. Under the assumption of a cooperative environment, various methods have been proposed to estimate these networks' boundaries using point clouds and graph representations. However, these methods fall short in networks operated and monitored remotely, prone to deception and data manipulation by someone in control of the surface layer. This paper fills the knowledge gap by investigating and comparing scale estimation techniques for small-world graphs subject to Byzantine faults, ultimately proposing a novel, robust algorithm. Our experimental results show that the proposed method accurately estimates the scale of such networks, even in highly hostile conditions.

This research focuses on developing a novel approach to estimate traffic parameters, particularly queue lengths, at signalized intersections using a nonparametric method. The proposed technique does not rely on specific probability distributions or parameter estimation and has been specifically designed to handle the underestimation of queue lengths commonly observed. A nonparametric estimator is used to capture the short-term behavior of queue lengths, which in turn informs predictive modeling. The predictive model employs an autoregressive conditional mean framework to anticipate future queue lengths based on historical data. A Bayesian hypothesis testing approach is applied to determine whether the nonparametric model successfully captures the underlying patterns of queue lengths. The proposed method's effectiveness has been validated through simulations and real-world data, demonstrating accurate predictions of future observations. The nonparametric estimator successfully captures the underlying distribution of historical data, according to the Bayesian hypothesis testing results. However, alternative modeling techniques, such as generalized linear models, have been identified as potential areas for further investigation.

In numerical simulations involving gravity, a common challenge is solving the complex, coupled nonlinear equations that arise as initial data constraints. These equations become even more difficult to solve when a rotating black hole spacetime is considered, an inherently unstable problem. To address this problem, we developed a new method, the Coupled Traceless Constraint Kernel (CTTK) solver, which reformulates the initial data constraints into a set of equations decoupled from each other. This reformulation expresses the geometric mass aspect and the momentum aspect as potential fields, allowing for a solution through the application of standard solver techniques, specifically the multigrid method, to solve the decoupled elliptic equations. When applied to a generic matter field, this solver reformulation results in a coupled system of equations that can be efficiently solved using existing solvers, such as the drift-diffusion algorithm. As an example, we utilized the CTTCK solver to create physically consistent initial data for a generic spacetime, including a rotating black hole surrounded a thick accretion disk.

This study investigates the unusual Nernst effect in MnNiNi nitrogen thin films, which were deposited using reactive magnetron sputtering and exhibited a diagonal Nernst effect at temperatures above their spontaneous transition temperature of approximately 175K. By combining Raman and neutron diffraction analyses, we determined that these films possessed an rhombohedral structure and demonstrated strong anisotropic antiferromagnetic ordering. Furthermore, we observed local ferromagnetic fluctuations at the B2a (fer) position, which were responsible for the diagonal Nernst effect, and discovered that the temperature at which the diagonal Nernst effect occurred was closely related to the spontaneous transition temperature. Additionally, we found that the diagonal Nernst effect disappeared during the antiferromagnetic to antiferromagnetic phase transition, but persisted during the antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic phase transition. Our findings highlight that MnNiNi nitrogen thin films possess significant potential for developing novel thermoelectric and spintronic devices.

The rapid advancement of machine learning and other forms of machine learning technologies is set to significantly transform the operation of next-generation research facilities, such as synchrotron light sources and free-electron lasers. These facilities, designed for the rapid and comprehensive investigation of material properties, produce vast quantities of data that would be nearly impossible for human researchers to manage alone. To address this challenge, this paper highlights the critical role of automated and algorithm-driven analysis in overcoming the limitations imposed by material samples' limitations and the overwhelming data generated by experimental facilities. We discuss how machine learning models can be utilized to facilitate the collection of extensive datasets and manage the complex operations of experiments, while also considering the specific requirements of various research platforms, including protein crystallography, operando studies, and materials science investigations. Ultimately, this paper aims to provide an actionable roadmap for effectively integrating and scaling machine learning-based tools in the field of research facilities and figure-out-how applications.

This work has solution and boundary regularity properties of sub-quadratic growth condition non-autonomous obstacle problems in the context of elliptic free boundary problems with variable growth rates examined. We establish that the problem's obstacles are sufficiently smooth near boundary points where solution behavior is well-behaved, and that solution behavior near these points is comparable to that of variables growth rate $p(t)=q(t)-1$ singular $p(q)$-Laplacian problems. We determine that points of variable rate $p(q)$ behave in a similar way to constant rate $p$ points, and that they are limited to a set with Hausdorff dimension at most $N-1/\max \{q\}$, providing a more comprehensive understanding of problems with variable growth rates.

We establish K-rationality for a specific class of ideals through GL_2 -Kummer theory, having first identified the ideal class group of K(\(\varpi\)) via local Artin map. This application further clarifies the nature of the GL_2 residue field.

We establish a precise isoperimetric relationship in the context of local variations of hypersurfaces that have a limited mean curvature, specifically identifying a term we call the isoperimetric residue. This residue, denoted as $\mathcal{R}$, characterizes the obstruction to achieving an optimal shape for a given amount of encased space and surface area. Furthermore, we define a smoothness condition, $\mathcal{SC}$, which indicates that local adjustments in area can lead to substantial changes in enclosed space. This condition is crucial for the development of a hypersurface that minimizes a certain isoperimetric problem within a larger space. It is proven that both having a limited mean curvature and satisfying the smoothness condition are equivalent conditions. Additionally, we demonstrate that any minimal surface within a given space can be found as an isoperimetric residue within a specific local configuration. These findings build upon the work of Cavallucci, Maggi, and Verdoom.

This research introduces a novel method for identifying material defects through electrical impedance tomography (EIT) and utilizes graph-based representations to streamline the inverse problem in self-monitoring applications. Furthermore, the study investigates the possibility of determining a defective area's dimensions, location, and orientation from EIT data. By leveraging graph-based representations in combination with an occlusion loss function and finite element analysis validation, material defects in composite materials can be accurately identified through neural network modeling. A 94% accuracy rate is achieved in reconstructing defects in a test sample, facilitating real-time defect detection for active self-sensing applications. Additionally, the network's ability to detect emerging material faults during operational use is highlighted, opening up exciting possibilities for composite material monitoring. However, a key limitation of the current model's reliance on static impedance data in the time domain is also acknowledged, underscoring the need for real-world implementation and exploration of time-varying signals in dynamic applications. Furthermore, a limitation of the current research in determining the defect's orientation from EIT data is also discussed, emphasizing the need for further investigation into this aspect of the model.

Elsholtz and one of us originally observed a striking pattern in our data: as the
number of twin prime candidates up to a given number x increases, the density of
actual twin primes within the same range tends to decrease. This intriguing phenomenon
inspired the title of one of our subsequent studies. However, further examination
revealed that the opposite trend applied, under certain conditions, suggesting an
unusual form of "intelligence" in mathematical sets that could potentially explain
this behavior. Building upon this concept, we devised an "intelligence" metric for
these sets and attempted to identify its underlying causes, which led us to develop
a theoretical model predicting this "intelligence" according to the range x.

This work explores the utilization of geometric quantities in tensor expressions within a general coordinate system to clarify the meaningfulness of certain second-rank tensors in a Euclidean space. It investigates the relationship between these tensors and positive or negative definite geometric quantities, providing a foundation for understanding more complex structures. Notably, this description can be extended to simplify the Schramm text's description of non-singular complex matrices using first and second geometric quantities, as well as confirming Legender's theorem regarding the interplay between these quantities.

The theory involving an scalar lepton-phobic Higgs, charged baryon number, and family symmetry naturally accounts for certain observational issues and results in a precise scale for neutrinos. The model predicts a specific ratio of approximately $10^{-27}$ for the decay of neutral kaons into three neutinos and two scalar leptons compared to the decay of neutral kaons into four neutinos. Due to the high suppression of the latter decay mode, this comparison can be compared to other decay channels, albeit with the note that the neutral kaon's average flight distance for such a decay is calculated to be roughly 25,000 km.

We demonstrate that in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory at the third level, all fourth-order stress-energy tensor components satisfy specific constraints that mirror those found in the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Toda conformal field theory. These constraints result in analogous fourth-order central charge indications forming an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ structure with levels $2$, $-1$, and $0$, and we observe that this pattern also applies to the four Toda theories with levels incorporating $i$.

We establish that Coxeter groups possess bi-automatic structures, building upon their previously proven bi-presentable status. This achievement can also be derived from the more specific bi-automatic nature of reflection groups, which in turn can be traced back to the compact geometric structures of right-angled Coxeter groups. The bi-automatic property of right-angled Coxeter groups further stems from their relationship with the bi-free group, from which it can again be deduced. The bi-automatic status of all these group types was further explored and compared to existing results, which established that both reflection and right-angled Coxeter groups have geometric structure, and that right-angled Coxeter groups are residually finite and have word problems solvable.

A leading approach in human rehabilitation involves using a motorized treadmill to retrain walking, but its effectiveness is limited due to users finding the experience confusing and frustrating. This study presents an investigation into creating an electrocorticogram (ECoG)-controlled treadmill that automatically adjusts based on a patient's steps and speed estimates. To assess this concept, we developed a method for determining step rates and velocities from cortical signals, utilizing hidden Markov models and support vector regression. This combination of techniques can accurately detect step rates and velocities with minimal error, but it requires careful consideration of the underlying statistical assumptions and their impact on results. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for more sophisticated, patient-friendly and intuitive mobility retraining systems.

We expand upon the concept of RAC graphs in this work, incorporating the preservation of isomorphism under the classification of RAC complexes through a specific type of splitting related to CAT(0) geometry. This classification is demonstrated to be equivalent to the classification of RAC graphs in the case of irreducible RAC complexes. Moreover, a specific RAC graph is identified that does not have hyperbolic geometry as a universal space.

In recent years, graph neural networks (GNNs) have led the way in graph-based machine learning advancements. Yet, most current approaches assume the underlying graph structure remains constant over time, disregarding its potential influence on predictive performance. We propose a novel efficient connectivity-based dynamic graph learning framework, REACH, to analyze and estimate evolving graph structures from multi-dimensional time series data. Each node in this model represents a temporal series, and the graph's connections reflect correlation patterns that can aid prediction tasks. We integrate a sparse non-negative factorization method, enhancing efficiency and interpretability, which allows us to efficiently compute the graph's adjacency matrix. To manage computational complexity, we employ a sparsity constraint, enabling scalable and iterative training of the model through a unified neural framework. Notably, we demonstrate that this approach can also capture highly dynamic graph patterns by removing the non-negativity constraint when necessary. We validate the effectiveness of REACH in various applications, including regression, classification, and sequential prediction tasks with static and dynamic graph scenarios.

Analyzing how organisms move in complex environments from video footage presents a significant challenge due to flowing media's many ways to represent reality. To investigate this difficulty, a study explores various computational methods, including traditional image analysis, representing content as a flow on a graph, and analyzing videos as high-dimensional spaces. A theoretical examination of a biological movement problem in video is developed, with a focus on understanding and applying these techniques to real-world data sets. Ultimately, this research aims to build a generative model, potentially incorporating neural manifolds, and examines the strengths and limitations of these approaches, particularly in capturing the structure of observed data and distinguishing between stationary and moving content.

This research delves into extending higher order methods, originally developed for finding fixed points, to solve large sparse linear systems of equations, an aspect critical in various computational fields. A specific iterative technique, HPMI, is identified as having an optimal computational kernel with very low communication requirements, making it well-suited for massive parallel processing. By applying theoretical analysis to HPMI and its proposed generalization, GMMI, both methods demonstrate the same strong linear scaling performance, offering alternatives to traditional iterative solvers like multigrid and Krylov subspace methods. GMMI, in particular, is shown to achieve rapid initial matrix factorization with improved stability and accuracy, presenting itself as a viable option for solving large sparse linear systems of equations.

We investigate the topological properties of one-dimensional systems with binary random disorders. Our study reveals that such disorders can induce an Anderson Chern insulator in a spinless Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model under specific conditions. Notably, we find that the size of the Anderson Chern insulator's phase is maximized when the high and low hopping lengths have a ten-to-one ratio and the probabilities of their occurrence are roughly equal. Our findings further suggest that the Anderson Chern insulator's phase is robust across a range of models and is even preserved in the presence of non-binary random disorders.

This research paper explores the connections between cut theories and linear logic, building upon the fundamental properties of cuts in categorical structures. We begin by examining the relevance of consques and consques+ in the 2-category of categories, functors, and natural transformations. Consequently, we investigate the role of tensor products and retro-tensor operations within various enriched categorical frameworks, including ordinary categories, $K$-enriched categories, and the realm of linear categories over a base $K$. We specifically analyze the behavior of cuts in linear categories over $K$, considering both additive and symmetric tensor variants. Notably, for the symmetric linear tensor case with the Knuth-Bendix completion algorithm, we derive a reduced and streamlined set of rewrite rules that amounts to 14 rules when the cardinality of $K$ is at least 2.

This presentation will delve into a thorough investigation of the Parameter Space of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), focusing on its Higgs sector. By utilizing the public, highly efficient HIGGUZ software, we have conducted an on-shell analysis of the MSSM Higgs sector, which features complex parameters. After accounting for one-loop corrections to the Higgs potential and the implementation of the DMRelict package, we determined the neutralino dark matter relic density. Key parameters defining the two-generation MSSM Supersymmetric Standard Model were then explored through the use of R-parity conserving settings. Subsequent analyses involved turning off specific parameters to examine their individual impacts. Subspace explorations were conducted where parameters were set within specific ranges while others were fixed. By visualizing key parameters in 3D and considering the impact of on-shell effects and the DM relic density, we gained a deeper understanding of the model's constraints. Ultimately, this study aims to push the boundaries of the Parameter Space, providing valuable insights for upcoming high-luminosity LHC experiments.

This work formulates the communication-efficient distributed contextual linear bandit problem across two distinct settings: a homogeneous one, where the context dimensions are consistent among agents, and a heterogeneous one, where context dimensions vary. We develop novel algorithms for both scenarios under both full-sharable and partially sharable setting protocols. In the shared protocol, where the master agent has access to all data, we achieve optimal context-independent sample complexity of $d/\phi$ in the homogeneous setting and a novel complexity measure of $(d/\phi)^{1+\epsilon}$ in the heterogeneous setting. In the non-sharable setting, where agents only share contextual features but not reward feedback, we achieve an optimal complexity of $d/\phi$ in the homogeneous setting and a novel complexity of $(d/\phi)^{1+\epsilon}$ in the heterogeneous setting, all while maintaining a high probability of success. These results highlight the first instance of achieving optimal learning in the homogeneous setting and the first instance of learning in the heterogeneous setting within a short amount of communication. Moreover, our work includes efficient context update protocols that allow the number of messages to remain polynomial in the dimension $d$ in the heterogeneous setting.

Our study utilizes the ALICE ALICE data from Pb-Pb collisions at a collision energy of $2.76$ TeV to investigate the event size of quark-gluon plasma produced in these collisions. We examine event shape engineering, focusing on the initial spatial anisotropy indicated by the elliptic flow ($v_2$) and particle momentum distribution analyzed in relation to secondary flow. Despite potential event shape variations, we found that average inclusive transverse momentum remains largely unchanged. Our observations support theoretical predictions regarding event size influence on quark-gluon plasma.

When considering the extremal gain of optimal power control in defining GDoF regions, we found that in networks with large K, it can provide an additional $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ DoFs to user far from interference and user experiencing intense interference, respectively, in comparison to binary power control. This result is established without considering dofs consumption for controlling power.

This study introduces an innovative multiple-time-step integration method to accelerate computational efficiency in multiple particle simulations, where the duration of particle collisions varies significantly. In this context, particles differ greatly in size and their interactions last different amounts of time; larger particles collide less frequently than smaller ones. While reductions in computational load have been observed with filtered simulations reducing particle differences, there's still considerable variability in collision durations that continues to impede simulations. We developed an algorithm for simulating multiple particles with varying collision durations, and found that this new method markedly decreases computational time compared to traditional approaches. Furthermore, this study reveals that specifying simulation time steps based on the duration of the smallest particles' collisions can be substituted with the duration of the largest particles' collisions, without negatively affecting either numerical stability or accuracy of results. This is regarded as another significant advancement contributing to the feasibility of multiple particle simulations.

This article presents a method to demonstrate that given any positive integer $a,b$, there are infinitely many prime numbers $p$ which are congruent to $1$ or $9$ modulo $11$ for which there are exactly $6$ distinct solutions to the equation $p^2+pa+a^2=qp$. Furthermore, we establish the criterion that within the field $\mathbb{F}_p$, the equation $x^2+x+1=0$ has two solutions if and only if $p$ is congruent to $1$ modulo $11$.

This project aims to simulate and improve the progress of a one-legged hopping robot navigating through soft ground. Initially, various soil types are ranked based on their stickiness, and then a geometric model is developed to predict their effect on the terrain. The model's accuracy is verified through lab experiments using different kinds of clay. Subsequently, a physics-based simulation of the robot's movement is created, incorporating the geometric model's ground behavior. After validating the simulation with real-world data, methods to minimize soil deformation are explored, and their efficacy is demonstrated.

In this paper, a consistent theoretical framework is established to study the properties of flexible mesons, allowing for variation in the radius of constituent quarks. The relevant quantities - the constituent quark radius, vector and tensor meson polarizabilities, and transition amplitudes - are computed using the linearized relativistic equation. Results obtained match experimental observations, specifically demonstrating that the radii of vector and tensor mesons are slightly smaller than their respective bosonic counterparts, and that vector and tensor polarizabilities are equal to one another. Additionally, it is found that the radii and polarizabilities of flexible mesons change linearly as the ratio of vector/tensor coupling constants deviates from its standard value of one.

This work investigates the challenges and strategies for constructing a comprehensive and organized representation of information networks, serving various purposes, from theoretical studies to practical applications in network routing and visualization. We examine three distinct approaches for deriving tree structures from network graphs, including the use of spanners, flow-based techniques, and gradient descent, to solve a specific optimization problem. Our proposed solutions leverage Delo's conjecture, proving that computing a specific type of network representation can be achieved efficiently, with minimal time and space complexity, or the use of flow-based methods in relation to the structure of acyclic graphs, providing robust representation with low distortion and time efficiency, or the application of gradient descent to create a dynamic and reusable type of tree representation, consumable with increased efficiency compared to original methods. Our framework enables the computation of a highly accurate and efficient tree representation of a particular network in nearly linear time, providing a robust and reusable structure for further analysis and visualization.

We investigate the impact of varying time scales on solving combinatorial problems using quantum annealing and quench dynamics in the exact cover algorithm. Our findings show that an intermediate time scale can facilitate a smoother transition from the quantum annealing solution to a quench dynamics solution, significantly boosting the probability of staying in the ground state compared to sudden quenching. This effect is directly linked to the complexity of the energy landscape and applies universally. As a result, a two-stage protocol emerges that leverages both dynamics: initially preparing a state closely related to the ground state through quantum annealing, then allowing it to evolve under a gradual quench. This discovery highlights the importance of examining both dynamics to fully utilize quantum computers for solving combinatorial problems.

Potential hindrances to achieving superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelate (NIO) have been thoroughly examined using a four-band model, taking into consideration its two effective fermi surfaces. Our research suggests that electron localization at the (Nb) site could be a critical factor in NIO's characteristics. A downfolding of the nickel four-band model to an effective two-band model reveals that electron delocalization between the (Nb) site and the Ni 3d shell might be crucial. We discovered a tiny hole-like carrier density in the (Nb) 4d shell, indicative of a tendency for electron accumulation rather than lack. This screening effect could be seen as a carrier density 'screening hypothesis'. The electron delocalization between the Ni 3d shell and the (Nb) 4d shell could potentially be obstructed due to insufficient oxygen processing, leading to oxidation and oxidation-induced phase separation, and explaining why NIO superconductivity has been difficult to achieve. To effectively produce NIO superconductors, it is essential to develop processes that promote electron delocalization between the Ni 3d shell and the (Nb) 4d shell.

This research aims to establish the density-dependent sound speed in dense stellar matter, taking into consideration the equation of state (EoS) and the onset of strange baryons within compact stars. The EoS is divided into two distinct density regimes: hadronic matter up to five times the nuclear saturation density ($5\rho_s$) and quark matter beyond this threshold. The transition between these two quark matter phases is modeled using theRandolph-Tjoelte light quark model, while the hadronic matter is described by theArnd-Haensel three-flavor hadron resonance gas model. The research reveals that a sound speed dropping below the nuclear saturation point leads to instability in compact stars, whereas an abruptly dropping sound speed beyond$5\rho_s$ results in a lack of neutron star quark cores. The research also demonstrates that incorporating a strange quark hadronic resonance, specifically $\Omega^-$, within the hadronic gas can delay the quark matter phase transition, potentially allowing for dense stellar matter with a quark core beyond$5\rho_s$.

Traditional quantum mechanics formalism is based on the Dirac state vector space, which can be equivalently described using the Compass state vector space. A key distinction between the two spaces is that the Compass state space incorporates the momentum operator's eigenstates, thereby expanding the state vector space. A comparative analysis of both spaces reveals their similarity in handling the Schrödinger equation and other fundamental operators, which can be expressed through transformation rules involving the position and momentum operators. Notably, certain properties such as the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and the Dirac bra-ket notation remain invariant or remain largely unchanged. However, both spaces exhibit different responses to compression and displacement operations, which can be modeled using Hamiltonian operators, resulting in varied expectation values, variance, and probability distributions. This difference in behavior may be attributed to the state's name, "Compass state," reflecting its response to compression and displacement operations compared to the standard state.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems, particularly in their outer regions. To better understand VSI, researchers utilized 3D global simulations to analyze how particle growth and dust settlement influence VSI development. According to simulation results, the size of solid particles can significantly impact the extent of VSI. In particular, when the solid growth ratio surpasses 0.1, vertical epicyclic frequency needs to increase by a factor of approximately three to four to enable significant development of VSI, primarily due to gas pressure generated by collisions between solid particles. In addition, the settling of dust in midplanes of disks contributes to VSI suppression through radiative effects. In radiative-less scenarios, the extent of VSI is found to depend on local conditions with minimal interdependence, but in radiative situations, VSI can trigger instabilities like the thermal wind instability and magnetorotational instability, leading to the rapid development of turbulence and efficient dust transport in a short period. In situations where gas conditions favor VSI development, the rate of dust transport found in simulations occurs much faster compared to existing models of dust evolution in protoplanetary disks.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. Notably, unless the described manifold has specific geometric properties, all harmonic functions of a certain growth rate have a fixed maximum value. The proof of this theorem relies on an alternative approach, diverging from the original method used in the established theorem's validation. As a consequence, it is possible to derive additional properties of harmonic functions and calculate specific integrals over the described manifold.

Recent advancements in neural backdoors have achieved static security guarantees, ensuring that data indistinguishable to the model will behave in a certain way under the model's predictions. Researchers have begun exploring complex, non-stereotypical trigger patterns, including things as subtle as watermarks or as intricate as watercolors. However, these trigger patterns must be considered fixed and known to the model during training, failing to account for their potential variability. In response, our research aims to establish dynamic backdoors in the absence of a predetermined pattern, knowing only that certain images will present a particular feature, in this case, a central average. Surprisingly, we discovered that a simple convolutional neural network can effectively distinguish these patterns, enabling the creation of a dynamic backdoor that acts in response to images containing a central average, regardless of their content. Furthermore, we prove the robustness of this backdoor in the face of perturbations and transformations, and provide the concept of an inverse trigger, demonstrating that even highly suspicious, non-natural patterns can activate the same behavior.

High-precision measurements from astrometric missions, such as Euclid and Gaia, allow for rigorous testing of gravitational theories, particularly through precise measurements of planetary and stellar motions. Precise models of their movements, relying on precise observations, are essential for comparing gravitational theories to empirical data, as even minor inaccuracies in these models can significantly skew interpretations. In this study, we assess various general relativistic effects, including gravitational redshift, light bending, and geodetic precession, using post-Newtonian formalism with precise calculations, loss function explorations, and Monte Carlo simulations. Analyzing the impact of position and velocity parameters on the precision of derived physical quantities, we find that the PPN parameter $\gamma$, which significantly influences light bending and geodetic precession, is the primary source of uncertainty in spectroscopic binaries and exoplanets, and may pose an issue for stellar movements. Moreover, a sub-percent level of precision in $\gamma$ is required for the reliable determination of stellar ages and a bias in parallax measurements of distant stars emerges when $\gamma$ is not accurately known, as seen with the Eridanus stellar stream when using Gaia-like data.

To provide an answer that encompasses human-like knowledge, it's essential to identify the fundamental nature of answers to open-domain commonsense questions. However, current answer-centric analyses fall short in capturing nuanced human knowledge, particularly in instances involving abstract concepts. To tackle this challenge, this research proposes a novel data format called semantic-related chains, which encapsulates both surface-level and deep, meaningful knowledge. Furthermore, this research introduces a new model that integrates chain-of-thought reasoning with attention mechanisms to capture the complex structure of human knowledge and enhance the analysis of open-domain commonsense question answering. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, yielding significant performance improvements over various baseline models. Additionally, careful examination of attention patterns reveals that models can focus on attention-related nuances, highlighting areas of strength and potential weakness in human knowledge. This analysis suggests that by incorporating chain-attention reasoning, we can develop a more comprehensive understanding of the nuances of open-domain commonsense question answering.

Astronomical environments can't be fully understood without a thorough understanding of molecular spectra, in particular those of molecules that exchange protons. Although the fundamental properties of many common space molecules are well-documented, a significant portion of spectral knowledge remains unexplored,特别是在cometary environments. Researchers should prioritize the examination of spectral gaps in space molecules, particularly those exchanging protons and containing oxygen, including H2O+, CO2+, and CO+. These molecules exchange protons present in cometary environments, whose compositions have been variably observed over time. Cometary environments also contain hydrogen-fluoride (HF) and phosphine (PH3), whose sources are still not fully understood. The examination of spectral gaps in these molecules is essential to gaining a comprehensive understanding of cometary environments, and should involve theoretical calculations and experimental validations, in particular high-resolution spectra that can be matched to observations. By doing so, scientists can better interpret the compositions of cometary environments and gain a deeper understanding of the fundamental properties of molecular spectra, in particular those of molecular cations, whose masses are significantly influenced by their electric charges.

In this paper, we address the heter数据 problem encountered in Federated Learning, specifically focusing on structure and distribution types. To tackle this challenge, we introduce the Stroll algorithm, a novel random walk method that operates on aggregation servers participating in the FedAvg process. The Stroll algorithm effectively navigates through locally stored data, selecting more representative clients for participation in model training. We demonstrate the versatility of this approach by applying it to both static and dynamic heter数据 scenarios, and through comprehensive experiments, we show that the Stroll algorithm enhances the performance of FedAvg by 20% to as much as 50% when dealing with strong heter数据. Furthermore, the additional computational cost incurred on aggregation servers is negligible, and the results hold true for learning tasks beyond neural networks.

This study investigates the impact of mandatory therapy for individuals who have been convicted, a policy that's designed to address behavioral issues and prevent recidivism through professional guidance and counseling. The research utilizes actual therapy treatment records from a prison in Georgia over a three-year period to examine the effects of this policy on mental health, based on individual characteristics and changes over time. A key research question concerns whether convicted individuals who undergo mandatory therapy show improvements in mental health compared to their peers who have been convicted but are exempt from this requirement. The results indicate that this policy has no significant effect on mental health, as measured by psychological testing administered while the individuals were in prison. Furthermore, the data reveals that individual responses to this policy are inconsistent, as certain features of the individuals predict psychological test scores improvements in some cases but also in others. The study discusses possible explanations for these results, considering alternatives to this policy's effectiveness prevention on mental health.

A persistent issue in medical image segmentation is the lack of pixel-level annotation. This study introduces a new regularization technique based on the expectation maximization (EM) algorithm to address this issue in semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed method uses data and pseudo-labels in an symmetric manner. It was found that this approach leads to better generalization. When tested on eight publicly available datasets using the KLD divergence and its robust variant, the proposed method outperformed top method. It also demonstrated superior stability in handling noisy labels. The code for the method is available online at this link: https://github.com/zhongshengzhang/EM_S3M.

Our study focuses on predicting chaotic chemical reaction outcomes, particularly in complex systems with numerous atoms, by applying and improving the LGNN model through a step-by-step graph neural network approach. Our findings show that the enhanced eLGNN model significantly outperforms the baseline model in prediction accuracy and exhibits higher interpretability by pinpointing key atoms influencing reactions. Furthermore, in predicting chemical reactions, we demonstrate that the eLGNN can accurately anticipate the results of a simulated X-ray experiment and may even help design such simulations in advance. In addition, we apply the eLGNN to real-world gas-phase reactions in laboratory settings and find that it excels at predicting reaction scattering based on laboratory data. Ultimately, our research provides a practical and advanced solution for predicting the dynamic behavior of chemical reactions and even complex reactions involving multiple atoms.

Our research establishes that if the family of distributions $\mathcal{P}$ is countably generated, and for any two distributions Q and P, the likelihood function exhibits a form of continuity, then for any sequence of distributions Q and P, and any path integral that is well-defined, with high probability, the following inequality holds:
